nameStory: This millipede earned its "black-and-gold" name from its striking color pattern of dark bands alternating with bright yellow, orange, or sometimes pink stripes. The "cherry" part of its alternate name comes from its remarkable defense mechanism — when threatened, it releases chemicals that smell exactly like cherry or almond extract!
description: The black-and-gold flat millipede is a large, eye-catching arthropod that can grow up to two inches long. Unlike earthworms, millipedes have many pairs of tiny legs and a segmented body that's flattened rather than round. This species displays bold stripes of black alternating with bright yellow, orange, or pink, making it one of the most colorful millipedes you'll encounter in New England forests.

idTips.label: Cherry scent when disturbed
idTips.description: When touched or threatened, releases a distinct sweet smell of cherry or almond extract — this chemical defense is unmistakable

idTips.label: Flattened body shape
idTips.description: Body is noticeably flat and wide rather than cylindrical, with a smooth, somewhat glossy texture

idTips.label: Bold striped pattern
idTips.description: Alternating bands of deep black with bright yellow, orange, or pink stripes running across each body segment

idTips.label: Large size
idTips.description: Can reach up to two inches in length, making it substantially larger than most other millipedes

idTips.label: Slow, deliberate movement
idTips.description: Moves in a wave-like motion with its many legs, much slower than centipedes, often curling into a spiral when disturbed

habitat: Look for these millipedes in deciduous and mixed forests with rich, moist leaf litter and decaying wood. They prefer areas with deep organic soil layers under oak, maple, and other hardwood trees. You'll often find them beneath fallen logs, under loose bark, or burrowing through the decomposing leaves on the forest floor.

seasonality.spring: Adults become active as soil warms, often found under logs and in leaf litter as they begin feeding on decomposing plant matter.
seasonality.summer: Most active period when you're likely to spot them crawling on the forest floor or climbing on rotting logs during humid evenings.
seasonality.fall: Still active but beginning to seek deeper shelter in preparation for winter, often found deeper in leaf litter piles.
seasonality.winter: Hidden deep in soil, under logs, or in other protected spots where they remain dormant until spring warmth returns.

funFact: This millipede is essentially a tiny chemical weapons factory — it produces hydrogen cyanide (the same compound used in gas chambers) and benzaldehyde as defense chemicals, but the sweet cherry scent makes it smell like you're baking a pie instead of encountering a toxic creature!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with other flat millipedes, but the cherry/almond scent when disturbed is a dead giveaway. Remember: if it smells like dessert when you touch it, you've found your black-and-gold flat millipede!
contextualKnowledge: Despite producing hydrogen cyanide, these millipedes pose no real danger to humans since they produce such tiny amounts. However, always wash your hands after handling them, and never rub your eyes after touching one — basic precautions that apply to handling any wild arthropod.
compareHints: This is the only Apheloria species commonly found in New England, but it can be distinguished from other flat millipedes in the cherry millipede family by its larger size and distinctive cherry scent. Other flat millipedes in the region are typically smaller, less colorful, and don't produce the characteristic sweet smell when disturbed.
